headings.title: Introduction to Adequate Diet and Core Principles
headings.content: An adequate diet provides all the necessary nutrients and energy required to maintain proper body functioning, support growth, and prevent deficiency diseases. The foundation of such a diet rests on four main principles: adequacy, balance, calorie control, and variety. Adequacy means consuming enough essential nutrients to meet daily physiological demands. Balance involves eating foods from different nutritional groups so that no single nutrient overpowers the others. Calorie control ensures that the energy intake matches the energy expenditure, preventing unwanted weight changes. Variety encourages a mix of different foods within each food group to lower the risk of nutrient toxicities or monotonous eating patterns. Nurses often use these core principles when counseling patients on how to build healthier plates using locally available food items.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content:
Macronutrients are the nutritional building blocks required in large amounts to supply energy, repair tissues, and regulate metabolic processes.

- **Carbohydrates**: The primary energy source for the body, especially the brain and central nervous system. Complex carbohydrates like whole grains and tubers offer sustained energy along with dietary fiber.
- **Proteins**: Essential for growth, tissue repair, immune function, and enzyme production. They are built from amino acids, some of which the human body cannot manufacture on its own.
- **Fats**: Also known as lipids, these compounds provide concentrated energy, protect vital organs, and assist in the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

A common misconception is that all dietary fats are harmful to health. In reality, unsaturated fats found in fish, nuts, and vegetable oils are vital for cardiovascular and cellular health.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Essential Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content:
Micronutrients consist of vitamins and minerals. Though the body requires them in much smaller quantities than macronutrients, they are indispensable for normal physiological function, immune defense, and bone health.

| Nutrient Type | Primary Function | Common Food Sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-soluble vitamins | Energy metabolism and cell maintenance | Citrus fruits, green leafy vegetables |
| Fat-soluble vitamins | Vision, blood clotting, and bone growth | Palm oil, liver, fish, eggs |
| Major minerals | Fluid balance and muscle contraction | Iodized salt, dairy, beans |
| Trace minerals | Oxygen transport and immune support | Red meat, shellfish, local legumes |

Deficiencies in these micronutrients lead to well-known deficiency states, such as anemia from lack of iron or night blindness from vitamin A shortage.

headings.title: The Role of Water and Hydration in Daily Nutrition
headings.content: Water is often considered the most critical nutrient for human survival. It makes up over half of total body weight and serves as the medium for virtually all cellular chemical reactions. Adequate hydration maintains blood volume, regulates body temperature through perspiration, lubricates joints, and helps flush out metabolic waste products through the kidneys. Dehydration occurs when fluid loss exceeds fluid intake, leading to symptoms like dry mouth, dizziness, dark urine, and confusion. Nurses must monitor fluid balance closely, especially in vulnerable groups like young children with gastroenteritis or elderly patients who may have a diminished sense of thirst.

headings.title: Dietary Guidelines and Food Guides in Nigeria
headings.content: Food guides translate complex nutritional science into practical, culturally appropriate advice for the general population. In Nigeria, dietary guidelines emphasize using locally grown food crops organized into food groups such as cereals and grains, roots and tubers, legumes, vegetables, fruits, animal proteins, and fats and oils. Local food guides promote the concept of food combinations—such as pairing beans with maize or rice—to achieve complete amino acid profiles when animal protein is scarce. Nurses use these food guides during health education sessions in community clinics to help families prepare balanced meals using affordable market ingredients.

headings.title: Nutritional Needs Across the Lifespan
headings.content: Nutritional requirements change dramatically as a person moves through different life stages. Infants require breast milk or specialized formula for rapid brain development and body growth. During pregnancy and lactation, women need extra calories, protein, iron, and folic acid to support fetal development and milk production. Childhood and adolescence demand high energy and nutrient intake to fuel growth spurts and bone mineralization. In contrast, older adults generally require fewer calories because their basal metabolic rate slows down, but they still need high amounts of calcium, vitamin D, and protein to prevent muscle wasting and bone loss.

headings.title: Assessing Nutritional Status and Dietary Intake
headings.content: Nutritional assessment helps identify individuals who are undernourished, overweight, or at risk for diet-related illnesses. Nurses use the ABCDE approach: Anthropometric measurements (height, weight, body mass index, and mid-upper arm circumference), Biochemical lab tests (such as serum albumin and hemoglobin levels), Clinical signs (inspecting hair, skin, eyes, and oral mucosa for deficiency signs), Dietary history (evaluating a 24-hour food recall or food frequency questionnaire), and Environmental or socioeconomic factors. Conducting these assessments early allows the healthcare team to catch malnutrition before it severely delays recovery.

headings.title: Nursing Interventions for Promoting Adequate Nutrition
headings.content: Promoting adequate nutrition is a core nursing responsibility in both hospital wards and community health settings. Nurses assist patients by calculating calorie needs, monitoring meal consumption, creating a clean and relaxing dining environment, and feeding patients who have physical limitations. For patients who cannot eat by mouth due to severe illness or swallowing difficulties, nurses manage enteral tube feedings or monitor parenteral nutrition lines. Furthermore, nurses provide tailored patient and family education, explaining how to modify diets for chronic conditions like hypertension or diabetes using affordable local food substitutes.
